facts.claim: "Super Freaky Girl" was produced by Dr. Luke and Malibu Babie, with Vaughn Oliver and Aaron Joseph also credited as producers.
The song interpolates Rick James's 1981 single "Super Freak", which James co-wrote with Alonzo Miller. Minaj had earlier sampled "Super Freak" on "Dilly Dally" from her 2007 mixtape Playtime Is Over.

Malibu Babie said she and two collaborators landed on the "Super Freak" sample and fine-tuned the beat for several hours. It then reached LunchMoney Lewis and was played for Minaj, who wrote the whole song within about 24 hours.
Malibu Babie became the first woman this century to debut at No. 1 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs as a producer, with this song.
Minaj previewed the song as "Freaky Girl" on social media in July 2022. Rick James's official account called the snippet a "banger".
Minaj asked fans to choose the title. She said legal issues kept her from using "Freaky Girl" or "Freak" (the fan-poll winner), so she settled on "Super Freaky Girl".
The track features Minaj's alter ego Nick James, named after Rick James. It is bass-heavy and opens with James's a cappella vocals.
The song debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. It was Minaj's first No. 1 as a solo artist and her 21st Hot 100 top 10.
It was the lead single from Minaj's fifth studio album Pink Friday 2 (Republic Records, December 8, 2023), and is certified double platinum in the US.
A "Queen Mix" of the song followed in September 2022, featuring JT, BIA, Katie Got Bandz, Akbar V and Maliibu Miitch. A Roman Remix was released six days after the original.

research.lineage: A raunchy, sample-based pop-rap record that reworks Rick James's funk hit "Super Freak" from a woman's point of view, in line with Minaj's tradition of pairing hip-hop with pop hooks.

draft:
The first voice on **Super Freaky Girl** isn't Nicki Minaj's. It's Rick James, a cappella, singing that she's alright, that girl's alright with him. Then the record takes the microphone away from him. In James's 1981 "Super Freak," co-written with Alonzo Miller, the freak was someone he watched and described. Here she does the describing, and she isn't waiting for anyone's approval.

Minaj has been circling this song a long time. She sampled "Super Freak" on "Dilly Dally" back on her 2007 mixtape *Playtime Is Over*. This time the spark came from producer Malibu Babie, who said she and two collaborators landed on the sample and spent hours fine-tuning the beat. It passed through LunchMoney Lewis to Minaj, who wrote the whole song in about a day. Dr. Luke, Vaughn Oliver and Aaron Joseph share the production credits. Even the alter ego she raps as, Nick James, tips a hat to the original.

The beat is bright and bass-heavy. A sustained low note holds the floor while a high, plucked synth pecks out a short staccato figure, and kick, snare and quick hi-hats keep a steady, driving pace. The mix is dry and close, with no reverb to hide in. That suits a voice this direct: mostly rapped and conversational, slipping into sung phrases, never padded with harmonies. It's just her, right up front.

The feeling here is pleasure, and the pleasure comes from being in charge. The chorus runs through everything she can do and lands on the man's side of it: "every time he leave me 'lone, he always tell me he miss it." His longing is the punchline, and then it becomes a chant, F-R-E-A-K spelled out like a cheer at a game she's already won. The verses move from the bedroom to the arena. "I got a princess face, a killer body, samurai mind" is a self-portrait in three quick strokes. The rivalry matters as much as the sex: an ex who went up against her and lost, imitators who can't be Nicki. The best joke is a résumé gag, "On applications, I write 'pressure'," a boast and a wink in the same breath. Desire and competition sit side by side, and neither one apologizes for the other.

The song debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, Minaj's first solo chart-topper. It also made Malibu Babie the first woman this century to debut at No. 1 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs as a producer. That's a fitting result for a record about who gets to tell the story.

You come away knowing how it feels when a song that once stared at a woman gets answered by her, louder and funnier and completely in control.
